tips.title: Split makes no comparisons
tips.body: Every comparison in a merge sort happens while **merging**. The splitting stage just halves lists and compares nothing. Saying so shows you know where the work happens, and it stops you inventing work that does not exist.

tips.title: Only the fronts are compared
tips.body: To merge two sorted lists, look at the **front item of each**, take the smaller, repeat. You never scan through a list. When one runs out, copy the rest across with no further comparisons.

tips.title: Each round halves the lists
tips.body: 8 items need 3 rounds, 16 need 4, 1024 need 10. Doubling the data adds only **one** round. Each round still looks at every item, so the work a little more than doubles, where bubble sort's roughly quadruples.

tips.title: Name the trade-off, not just the speed
tips.body: "Merge sort is faster" is only half the comparison. The other half is **memory**: merge sort builds new lists as it merges, so it needs extra space, while bubble sort swaps in place.

why.matters:
Merge sort is the second of the two sorts AQA names, and it is here for contrast: it solves the same problem by a completely different route, and the route is the point.

Rather than walking the list again and again, it **splits** until every piece is one item — and a one-item list is already sorted, for free — then builds the answer back up by merging pairs. That pattern, divide and conquer, turns up far beyond sorting, and the reason it wins is that the merging is cheap while the splitting halves the problem every time.

examples.title: Why splitting stops at one
examples.body:
Halve **6, 2, 9, 4, 1, 7, 3**, halve the halves, and keep going: after 3 rounds you have 7 lists of one item each. There is nothing to do to them. **A list of one item is already in order**, which is the base case the whole algorithm rests on.

An odd number is not a problem — one half is simply one shorter, and the 6 at the front is left on its own until the next round. The splitting does no sorting whatever; it exists to reach the point where sorting is free.

visual.alt: A table of the splitting stage of a merge sort on seven numbers: each round halves every list from the row above until every list holds a single item, with the lone 6 left on its own until the next round

examples.title: Why merging only ever looks at the fronts
examples.body:
Two sorted lists, **1 4 6** and **2 3 9**. Compare the front of one with the front of the other, take the smaller, and repeat. When one list runs out, the rest of the other goes straight on the end.

It works because each list is already in order, so the smallest item left is certain to be at the front of one of them — nothing further along can beat it. That is why merging is quick, and why the exam tests the merge rather than the split: the merge is where the sorting actually happens.

visual.alt: A table tracing the merge of two sorted lists of three numbers: at each step the two front items are compared and the smaller is taken, and when one list empties the remainder of the other is added to the end

examples.title: Why two people sort a pile of paper faster than one
examples.body:
Split the pile, hand half to somebody else, and you both sort a smaller pile. The only new work is putting the two sorted halves together at the end, and that part is easy: look at the top sheet of each, take the earlier one.

That is merge sort, and it is why the algorithm is everywhere that the data is large or the work is shared out — the pieces can be sorted independently, in any order, and merged whenever they are ready. Bubble sort cannot be divided up like that at all, because every pass depends on the one before it.

boxes.title: Sort each
boxes.body: Separately, and at the same time.

visual.alt: Four boxes round a centre reading one unsorted pile: split it into two piles, sort each separately and at the same time, compare the top sheets and take whichever comes first, and finish with one sorted pile

steps.title: Divide and conquer
steps.body:
Bubble sort walks the same list over and over. Merge sort does something completely different: it **splits the problem up**.

The idea has two halves:

1. **Divide.** Split the list in half, then split each half in half, and keep going until every list holds a **single item**. A list of one item is already sorted, which is the point.
2. **Conquer, by merging.** Take the small sorted lists in pairs and **merge** each pair into one sorted list. Repeat until only one list is left.

Nothing is compared until the merging starts. All the work of sorting happens on the way back up.

steps.title: Merging two sorted lists
steps.body:
Merging is the part that does the sorting, and it is the part the exam tests. The rule is short:

> Look at the **front item of each list**. Take the smaller one and put it into the new list. Repeat. When one list runs out, copy the rest of the other straight across.

The crucial point is that you only ever look at the **front** of each list. You never scan through them. That is why merging is fast.

Fronts are 6 and 9. 6 is smaller, so take it → [2, 4, 6]
The first list is empty, so copy the rest of the second across → [2, 4, 6, 9]

steps.title: The merging stage
steps.body:
Now the way back up for **6, 2, 9, 4, 1, 7, 3**. Each round merges back exactly the lists the splitting produced, in pairs. A list with no partner, like the lone **6** here, simply waits for the next round.

Read the last row: one list, in order. That is the sorted result.

steps.title: How many rounds of merging
steps.body:
Because each round **halves** the number of lists, the number of rounds grows very slowly with the length of the list.

A list of 8 splits into 8 single items, which merge into 4 lists, then 2, then 1: **3 rounds**. A list of 16 needs 4 rounds. Doubling the list adds only **one** round. Each round still looks at every item, so the work a little more than doubles (about $n \log_2 n$ comparisons), where bubble sort's roughly quadruples.

That is the whole reason merge sort beats bubble sort on long lists, and it is what an efficiency question is after.

steps.title: Going deeper: merge sort against bubble sort
steps.body:
A comparison question is worth several marks, and the answer has a shape.

**Speed.** Bubble sort's comparisons grow with $n^2$; merge sort's grow far more slowly, because each round halves the number of lists and there are only about $\log_2 n$ rounds. For 1024 items bubble sort needs about half a million comparisons and merge sort about ten thousand.

**Memory.** This is the trade-off. Merge sort **builds new lists as it merges**, so it needs extra memory roughly the size of the original list. Bubble sort swaps items where they are and needs almost none.

**Consistency.** Merge sort takes the same number of rounds whatever order the list starts in. Bubble sort is much faster on an already sorted list, because the swapped flag stops it after one pass, and much slower on a reversed one.

So: merge sort is faster on long lists but uses more memory; bubble sort is simpler and can win on short or nearly sorted lists.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Merge sort is **divide and conquer**: split until every list holds one item, then merge pairs back together.
- A one-item list is **already sorted**, which is why splitting stops there.
- **No comparisons happen while splitting.** All the work is in the merges.
- To merge two sorted lists, compare only their **front items**, take the smaller, and copy the leftovers across when one runs out.
- Each round **halves** the number of lists, so a list of 8 needs 3 rounds and 16 needs 4. Doubling the list adds one round.
- Merge sort is much **faster** than bubble sort on long lists, but needs **extra memory** for the lists it builds.
- On 6, 2, 9, 4, 1, 7, 3: 3 levels of splitting, then 3 rounds of merging to reach 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Divide first.** The list **5, 2, 8, 1** is halved into **5, 2** and **8, 1**. Each of those is halved again, giving the single items **5**, **2**, **8** and **1**. A list of one item is already sorted, so the splitting stops there, and no comparisons have been made yet.

**Then merge.** Merging **5** with **2** compares the two fronts and gives **2, 5**. Merging **8** with **1** gives **1, 8**. Now merge those two sorted lists: compare the fronts 2 and 1 and take **1**; compare 2 and 8 and take **2**; compare 5 and 8 and take **5**; the first list is now empty, so the **8** is copied across without a comparison. The result is **1, 2, 5, 8**. Every comparison happened during the merging, none during the splitting.

questions.prompt: Compare merge sort and bubble sort, and say which you would choose to sort a list of one million items.
questions.solution: Bubble sort compares every neighbouring pair on every pass, so its comparisons grow with the square of the list length. Merge sort halves the number of lists at every round, so it needs only about log to base 2 of n rounds and is far faster on long lists. The trade-off is memory: merge sort builds new lists as it merges and so needs extra memory roughly the size of the original, while bubble sort swaps items in place and needs almost none. Bubble sort is also simpler to write and finishes in a single pass on an already sorted list. For a million items the speed difference is overwhelming, so merge sort is the right choice, provided the extra memory is available.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Bubble sort** compares every neighbouring pair on every pass, so for $n$ items it makes about $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ comparisons and the work grows with the **square** of the length. **Merge sort** halves the number of lists at every round, so it needs only about $\log_2 n$ rounds and grows far more slowly.

The trade-off is **memory**. Merge sort builds new lists as it merges, so it needs extra space roughly the size of the original list. Bubble sort swaps items where they sit and needs almost none. Bubble sort is also **simpler to write**, and on an already sorted list its swapped flag finishes the job in a single pass, which merge sort cannot match.

For **one million items** the difference is overwhelming: bubble sort would need something like $5 \times 10^{11}$ comparisons, while merge sort needs around 20 rounds. **Merge sort** is the right choice, as long as the machine has the extra memory it needs.

examTechnique.body:
Merge sort questions come in two shapes: trace it, or compare it with bubble sort. For a trace, draw the splitting as a tree or as rows of lists, then the merging as rows back up. Show every level. A question asking for the lists *after the second round of merging* is testing whether you traced it, so do not jump to the sorted answer.

When merging, compare only the **front** items and say so. Writing out the fronts you compared shows the method.

A comparison has three parts: speed, memory and consistency. Speed alone is only a third of it; the memory point, that merge sort builds new lists while bubble sort swaps in place, is the one easiest to leave out.
examinerErrors: Saying comparisons happen while splitting. Splitting makes none; every comparison is in a merge.
Sorting each half in your head instead of merging it. The merge is the method being tested.
Comparing every item of one list with every item of the other. Only the front items are compared.
Forgetting to copy the leftovers across when one list runs out.
Claiming merge sort finishes early on an already sorted list. It does the same rounds whatever the order; bubble sort is the one that stops early.
Giving speed as the only difference from bubble sort. The extra memory merge sort needs is the other half of the comparison.
Saying an odd-length list cannot be split. One half simply takes the extra item.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer traces both stages with every level written out, and states that splitting makes no comparisons. It describes merging as comparing the front items and copying leftovers across, and can count the comparisons a merge needs. On efficiency it explains that halving the lists gives about $\log_2 n$ rounds against bubble sort's $n^2$ comparisons, puts numbers to it, and then gives the trade-off: merge sort needs extra memory, bubble sort sorts in place and can finish in very few passes on a nearly sorted list.
